SUBTYPE-FAMILY WINDOW DISCLOSURE (2026-10-04): the authored corpus already registers mixed-urinary-incontinence to depressive-disorder (rank 1; PMIDs 39600349, 39393464, 41076405) and overactive-bladder to depressive-disorder (rank 1; PMIDs 42222871, 37356462, 38108212), so this is the THIRD parallel subtype window to the same target; the three windows share no PMID, are one subtype-family evidence set read per subtype, and may not be pooled or treated as independent corroboration of one another. The anchors registered here measure urinary incontinence broadly and do not isolate the stress subtype, so the claim's exposure is mapped onto broad-urinary-incontinence evidence and that mapping is not reversible; subtype-specific claims require subtype-specific evidence.

DIRECTION DISCLOSURE carried on the face of the edge: both pooled anchors synthesize cross-sectional or case-control studies, and the single located prospective cohort measured the claimed direction as a NULL (1.03, 0.75-1.42) while finding the reverse direction positive (1.46, 1.08-1.97), so the association is registered with direction unresolved and may not be read as evidence that the incontinence produced any individual's depression.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Authoring registers this relationship only as the population-level association the located urinary-incontinence literature supports. A 2020 meta-analysis of 12 articles and 31,462 participants found the urinary-incontinence group's depression and anxiety levels significantly higher than the non-incontinent group (pooled odds ratio 1.73, 95 percent CI 1.64-1.82, I-squared 75.5 percent), with the depression subgroup at 1.95 (95 percent CI 1.82-2.10, I-squared 64.3 percent) and the anxiety subgroup at 1.54 (95 percent CI 1.43-1.65, I-squared 59.2 percent), and its authors state that larger sample sizes and more high-quality studies are needed (PMID 32552169); a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of the 8 studies reporting a binary outcome on validated scales pooled depression prevalence in women with urinary incontinence at 18 percent (95 percent CI 11-25 percent), with illiteracy (OR 1.34, 1.01-1.78), caesarean delivery (OR 1.48, 1.30-1.70), obesity (OR 1.37, 1.19-1.58), more than three children (OR 1.26, 0.98-1.62), comorbidity (OR 1.32, 1.16-1.49, I-squared 85.3 percent), smoking (OR 1.58, 0.99-1.92) and single, divorced or widowed status (OR 1.67, 1.45-1.92) as associated factors, and its authors expressly recommend future study of the CAUSAL association (PROSPERO CRD42023418779; PMID 39501253); and the single located prospective cohort — 5,820 community-dwelling women followed across 1996-2003 waves of the Health and Retirement Study, mean age 59.3 years, 6-year cumulative incidences of depression 11 percent and incontinence 21 percent — found major depression associated with incident incontinence (adjusted odds ratio 1.46, 95 percent CI 1.08-1.97) while incontinence was NOT associated with incident depression (adjusted odds ratio 1.03, 95 percent CI 0.75-1.42), so in the one design that can speak to temporal order the claimed direction is NULL and the reverse direction is positive (PMID 19716547). The registered claim is the narrowest these anchors jointly permit: urinary-incontinence populations carry a higher prevalence and odds of concurrent depression, with direction unresolved and with the only prospective evidence running against the registered direction.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation of depressive disorder under 38 CFR 3.310 is established for any individual by these anchors: the pooled evidence is cross-sectional or case-control and cannot establish that depression follows incontinence in time, the one located prospective cohort measured the claimed direction as a null (adjusted odds ratio 1.03, 95 percent CI 0.75-1.42) while finding the reverse direction positive (1.46, 1.08-1.97), and none of the anchors separates the association from shared and bidirectional drivers — obesity, parity and caesarean delivery, age, diabetes and other comorbidity, smoking, and the incontinence-associated sleep disruption, activity restriction, embarrassment and stigma that can depress mood without being measured. The anchors also measure urinary incontinence as a category rather than the stress subtype, so the exposure definition itself is a mapping. Individual claims require independently established stress urinary incontinence with its diagnostic basis (history, examination, urodynamic or leakage documentation), a separately established depressive disorder with a dated course, a chronology that can speak to direction, objective records of pelvic-floor, neurologic, medication and metabolic contributors, and documented exclusion of the reverse pathway and competing depression etiologies before any attribution.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized burden-and-stigma pathway: leakage-related embarrassment, fear of odor and detection, activity restriction and social withdrawal, continence-product burden, nocturia-related sleep disruption and loss of autonomy are held to act as chronic stressors that raise depressive-symptom burden; the pathway is stated as hypothesized rather than established because the pooled anchors are cross-sectional and the single located prospective cohort's claimed-direction estimate is a null, so no located design isolates this cascade in an individual.
causalMechanism.secondaryVector: The reverse and bidirectional pathways are at least as plausible on the located evidence: depression is prospectively associated with incident incontinence (adjusted odds ratio 1.46, 95 percent CI 1.08-1.97; PMID 19716547), plausibly through inactivity, weight gain, psychotropic medication effects and altered symptom reporting, and shared risk factors (obesity, parity and caesarean delivery, age, diabetes, smoking) drive both conditions; the located designs cannot separate these routes from the registered direction.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on two systematic reviews and meta-analyses plus the single located prospective cohort, and deliberately not beyond them. The pooled association is moderate and directionally undetermined: pooled odds ratio 1.73 (95 percent CI 1.64-1.82, I-squared 75.5 percent; depression subgroup 1.95, 1.82-2.10) across 12 articles and 31,462 participants, with the study's own authors calling for larger and higher-quality studies (PMID 32552169), and pooled depression prevalence 18 percent (95 percent CI 11-25 percent) across 8 validated-scale studies whose authors recommend future study of the causal association (PMID 39501253). The prospective anchor is registered as the edge's DIRECTION COUNTERWEIGHT because it answers the temporal question the pooled designs cannot and answers it against the registered direction: depression predicted incident incontinence (adjusted odds ratio 1.46, 95 percent CI 1.08-1.97) while incontinence did not predict incident depression (adjusted odds ratio 1.03, 95 percent CI 0.75-1.42; PMID 19716547). Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual; the anchors measure urinary incontinence as a category rather than the stress subtype; the demographic and clinical correlates the 2024 review quantifies (obesity, caesarean delivery, parity, comorbidity, smoking, illiteracy, marital status) are shared drivers the located designs do not control; and all three anchors remain unverified pending qualified-human citation verification under docs/citation-verification-sop.md; this suggestion, its registry lockstep and its adjacency node landed together on 2026-10-04 as batch 95 of the D1 draft-authoring series.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Design and direction: two of the three anchors synthesize cross-sectional or case-control studies, the pooled odds ratio carries I-squared 75.5 percent heterogeneity, and the only located prospective cohort measured the claimed direction as a positive null (1.03, 0.75-1.42) while finding the reverse direction positive (1.46, 1.08-1.97), so no located design establishes that incontinence precedes depression and onset chronology cannot be derived from the pooled estimates. Exposure-definition mapping: the located anchors measure urinary incontinence as a category, not the stress subtype, and two of the three anchors are women-only samples, so subtype- and sex-specific applicability is not established and the mapping is not reversible to other incontinence types; the sibling subtype windows registered in this corpus rest on disjoint anchors and cannot be pooled with this evidence set. Measurement and confounding: depression was ascertained through different validated scales across the pooled studies (the 2024 review pools only binary-outcome studies for poolability, and its strongest heterogeneity, I-squared 85.3 percent, attaches to comorbidity rather than to continence severity), and none of the anchors controls the full shared-driver set — obesity, parity and caesarean delivery, age, diabetes and other comorbidity, smoking, marital and socioeconomic status. No individual-level exposure-response: no located anchor quantifies leakage frequency, volume or duration against individual depressive outcomes, and none reports mood after continence treatment.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: The reverse and bidirectional pathway: depression predating and prospectively predicting incident incontinence (adjusted odds ratio 1.46, 95 percent CI 1.08-1.97 in the located prospective cohort), through inactivity, weight gain, psychotropic medication effects or altered symptom reporting

Shared risk factors for both conditions — obesity, parity and caesarean delivery, advancing age, diabetes and other comorbidity, smoking, and marital or socioeconomic status — all quantified as associated factors in the located 2024 review

Other established depressive-disorder etiologies unrelated to continence, including prior depressive episodes, bereavement, substance use, thyroid or other endocrine disease, medication effects and primary psychiatric illness

Concurrent pelvic-floor, urologic and neurologic conditions (pelvic organ prolapse, overactive bladder, mixed incontinence, neuropathy) that may drive both the leakage and the distress and are not separated by the located anchors
General illness burden and sleep disruption (nocturia, chronic pain, continence-product burden) misread as a continence-specific mood pathway
Medication effects (for example anticholinergics, antidepressants, diuretics) that alter continence, mood, or both

evidenceGaps: Design and direction: both pooled anchors synthesize cross-sectional or case-control studies (12 articles, 31,462 participants, odds ratio 1.73, 95 percent CI 1.64-1.82, I-squared 75.5 percent; 8 validated-scale studies, prevalence 18 percent, 95 percent CI 11-25 percent), and the single located prospective cohort measured the claimed direction as a null (1.03, 0.75-1.42) while finding the reverse direction positive (1.46, 1.08-1.97), so no located design establishes that incontinence precedes depression.

Exposure-definition mapping: the anchors measure urinary incontinence as a category rather than the stress subtype, so the exposure is mapped onto the subtype identity and the mapping is not reversible; subtype-specific claims require subtype-specific evidence, and the sibling subtype windows registered in this corpus rest on disjoint anchors and are not independent corroboration.

Population scope: the 2024 review pools women only and the prospective cohort is a 5,820-woman sample (mean age 59.3 years), while the 2020 meta-analysis pools mixed populations without stress-subtype stratification, so sex- and subtype-specific applicability is not established.

Confounding: none of the anchors controls the full shared-driver set the located reviews themselves quantify — obesity, caesarean delivery, parity above three, comorbidity (I-squared 85.3 percent), smoking, illiteracy and marital status — and none measures the behavioral burden (activity restriction, stigma, sleep disruption) that the hypothesized pathway posits.

No individual-level exposure-response or treatment data: no located anchor quantifies leakage frequency, volume or duration against individual depressive outcomes, and none reports depressive outcomes after continence treatment, so dose-response and reversibility are unmeasured.
suggestions.rationale: Authoring registers the next-five backlog window identified by scripts/report-authoring-backlog.js, opening the rank-1 stress-urinary-incontinence to depressive-disorder route as batch 95 of the D1 draft-authoring series on 2026-10-04. The located evidence quantifies a population association between urinary incontinence and concurrent depression — a 2020 meta-analysis of 12 articles and 31,462 participants (pooled odds ratio 1.73, 95 percent CI 1.64-1.82, I-squared 75.5 percent; depression subgroup 1.95, 1.82-2.10; anxiety subgroup 1.54, 1.43-1.65; PMID 32552169) and a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 validated-scale studies (pooled depression prevalence 18 percent, 95 percent CI 11-25 percent; associated factors including obesity, caesarean delivery, comorbidity, smoking and marital status; PROSPERO CRD42023418779; PMID 39501253) — and the edge is deliberately ASSOCIATION_ONLY with the DIRECTION COUNTERWEIGHT carried on its face: the only located prospective cohort (5,820 women, Health and Retirement Study waves 3-6) found depression predicted incident incontinence (adjusted odds ratio 1.46, 95 percent CI 1.08-1.97) while incontinence did NOT predict incident depression (adjusted odds ratio 1.03, 95 percent CI 0.75-1.42; PMID 19716547). No located anchor establishes that stress urinary incontinence caused or aggravated any individual's depressive disorder, which is why the classification carries NOT_ESTABLISHED etiological consensus and NOT_ASSERTED probability alignment rather than any stronger reading. Window discipline: the authored corpus already registers mixed-urinary-incontinence to depressive-disorder (rank 1; PMIDs 39600349, 39393464, 41076405) and overactive-bladder to depressive-disorder (rank 1; PMIDs 42222871, 37356462, 38108212), so this is the THIRD parallel subtype window to the same target; the three windows share no PMID, are one subtype-family evidence set read per subtype, and may not be pooled or treated as independent corroboration. This is the only registered window from stress-urinary-incontinence, and a future depression-first window (depressive-disorder to stress-urinary-incontinence) or a second continence-to-mood path would require npm run audit:crg redundancy adjudication before authoring. Scope discipline: the anchors measure urinary incontinence broadly rather than the stress subtype and the two women-only anchors bound the population; the exposure-to-subtype mapping is disclosed on the face of the edge and is not reversible. The route's anchors (PMID 32552169, PMID 39501253, PMID 19716547) were confirmed absent from the registry and cleared by source-status preflight with zero blocking flags on 2026-10-04; they enter verified:false pending qualified-human citation verification under docs/citation-verification-sop.md, and the relationship row, the three source entities and the graph adjacency node were registered in lockstep with this suggestion on 2026-10-04. Sibling-window precedent: the three subtype-family windows are ordinary draft windows; none is published, and none asserts an individual nexus.

sourceReferences.citation: Cheng S, Lin D, Hu T, Cao L, Liao H, Mou X, Zhang Q, Liu J, Wu T. Association of urinary incontinence and depression or anxiety: a meta-analysis. J Int Med Res. 2020 Jun;48(6):300060520931348. doi:10.1177/0300060520931348. PMID 32552169.
sourceReferences.note: Primary association anchor: meta-analysis of 12 articles and 31,462 participants, registered as this edge's POOLED-ODDS anchor because it is the largest located quantification of the incontinence-depression association: pooled odds ratio 1.73 (95 percent CI 1.64-1.82) with I-squared 75.5 percent, depression subgroup 1.95 (1.82-2.10, I-squared 64.3 percent), anxiety subgroup 1.54 (1.43-1.65, I-squared 59.2 percent), and higher depression and anxiety regardless of age (1.59, 1.29-1.95 and 1.98, 1.62-2.43). Only the depression member is relied on here. LIMITATIONS CARRIED: the pooled studies are cross-sectional or case-control, the exposure is urinary incontinence as a category without the stress subtype, the reported odds ratio summarizes group-level prevalence rather than incident risk, and the authors themselves state that larger sample sizes and more high-quality studies are needed. Mapping approval is not citation verification; this source enters verified:false pending separate qualified-human citation review.
